sourceLesson: Backend LLD: Concurrency-2: Executors and Futures

questions.title: `ProcessPoolExecutor` over `ThreadPoolExecutor`?
questions.question: Which is the best use case for ProcessPoolExecutor over ThreadPoolExecutor?

options.optionText: Waiting on 5 API calls with sleep/network delay
Reading multiple files from disk
Performing heavy numerical computation on 4 independent large datasets
Fetching 10 web pages concurrently

questions.title: `ProcessPoolExecutor` speed up an I/O-bound task like web scraping, compared to `ThreadPoolExecutor`
questions.question: Why doesn't ProcessPoolExecutor speed up an I/O-bound task like web scraping, compared to ThreadPoolExecutor?

options.optionText: ProcessPoolExecutor doesn't support .map()
The GIL blocks all network calls in processes
Processes cannot perform network requests
There's no computation to parallelize — the bottleneck is waiting, and processes add extra startup/communication overhead for no benefit

questions.title: True or False: Using ThreadPoolExecutor automatically protects shared variables from race conditions (like counter += 1 from multiple threads).
questions.question: True or False: Using ThreadPoolExecutor automatically protects shared variables from race conditions (like counter += 1 from multiple threads).

options.optionText: True — executors serialize all writes automatically
False — executors only manage task launching/collection; shared-state protection still needs tools like Lock

questions.title: What is `results`, and in what order, once this finishes?
questions.question:
What is results, and in what order, once this finishes?
```python
import time
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

def work(n):
    time.sleep(n)
    return n

with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=3) as executor:
    results = list(executor.map(work, [3, 1, 2]))
print(results)
```

options.optionText: Raises a TimeoutError
[2, 1, 3] — random order
[1, 2, 3] — sorted by finish time
[3, 1, 2] — same order as input list

questions.title: A student benchmarks CPU-heavy work and is confused why threads didn't help. Identify the flaw in their reasoning.
questions.question:
A student benchmarks CPU-heavy work and is confused why threads didn't help. Identify the flaw in their reasoning.

```python
def cpu_heavy(n):
    return sum(i * i for i in range(n))

with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as executor:
    list(executor.map(cpu_heavy, [50_000_000] * 4))
```

"I used 4 workers for 4 tasks, so this should be 4x faster than sequential."

options.optionText: max_workers=4 should be max_workers=1 for correctness
executor.map doesn't support functions with numeric arguments
The code has a syntax error, so it never runs
This is CPU-bound work; the GIL means only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time, so threads don't overlap computation — ProcessPoolExecutor is needed instead

questions.title: You're processing 4 large video files, applying a CPU-intensive filter to each, independently. Which is the better choice and why?
questions.question: You're processing 4 large video files, applying a CPU-intensive filter to each, independently. Which is the better choice and why?

options.optionText: Doesn't matter, both give identical performance
ThreadPoolExecutor — video processing is I/O-bound
Neither — must be done sequentially
ProcessPoolExecutor — CPU-bound work benefits from separate GILs per process, allowing true parallel computation across cores

questions.title: `ThreadPoolExecutor` task that sometimes throws an exception. You use `executor.map()` instead of `submit()`
questions.question: You have a ThreadPoolExecutor task that sometimes throws an exception. You use executor.map() instead of submit() + individual futures. What happens when you iterate over the results and one task failed?

options.optionText: map() cannot raise exceptions, only submit() can
map() skips the failed task and continues with the rest
The failed task's result is silently None
The exception is raised at the point of iteration when you reach that failed task's result, potentially stopping your loop from processing remaining results unless wrapped in try/except
None, until the task finishes
The result of fn(arg) directly
A new thread object
A Future object representing work in progress

questions.title: `.done()` and `.result()`
questions.question: Which statement about .done() and .result() is correct?

options.optionText: .done() never blocks; .result() blocks until the result is available
Both block until the task finishes
.done() blocks; .result() never blocks
Both return True/False depending on task status

questions.title: `threading.Thread`'s target function
questions.question: A raw threading.Thread's target function raises an exception. What happens?

options.optionText: The thread silently retries the function
The exception prints to the terminal but the main thread has no way to catch or react to it
The program crashes immediately
The exception propagates to the main thread automatically

questions.title: `Future` handle an exception
questions.question: How does a Future handle an exception raised inside the worker function?

options.optionText: It ignores the exception completely
It crashes the executor immediately
It logs the exception and returns None
It stores the exception and re-raises it when .result() is called

questions.title: executor.map(fn, iterable)
questions.question: What guarantee does executor.map(fn, iterable) give you about result order?

options.optionText: Only the first completed result is returned
Order is undefined/random
Results come back in the same order as the input iterable, regardless of finish order
Results come back in the order tasks finish

questions.title: A student wrote this to collect driver locations. What does it get wrong relative to today's lecture taught?
questions.question:
A student wrote this to collect driver locations. What does it get wrong relative to what today's lecture taught?
```python
import threading
results = []

def fetch_and_store(driver_id):
    location = fetch_driver_location(driver_id)
    results.append(location)

threads = [threading.Thread(target=fetch_and_store, args=(d,)) for d in drivers]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()
```

options.optionText: threading.Thread cannot take args
t.join() will deadlock
This code will throw a syntax error
This works, but relies on a manually shared list instead of ThreadPoolExecutor/Future to collect results and handle errors cleanly

questions.title: Find the bug: the student wants to catch the error from a failed task, but the `except` block never triggers, even though `fetch_driver_location("D103")` is known to raise `ConnectionError`.
questions.question:
Find the bug: the student wants to catch the error from a failed task, but the except block never triggers, even though fetch_driver_location("D103") is known to raise ConnectionError.
```python
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=1) as executor:
    future = executor.submit(fetch_driver_location, "D103")

try:
    print(future.done())
except ConnectionError as e:
    print(f"Fetch failed: {e}")
```

options.optionText: The with block suppresses all exceptions
ConnectionError cannot be caught inside a with block
The exception is only raised when .result() is called — .done() never raises, it only reports status
executor.submit doesn't accept string arguments

questions.title: You're building a system that downloads 100 images from different URLs. Which executor should you use, and why?
questions.question: You're building a system that downloads 100 images from different URLs. Which executor should you use, and why?

options.optionText: ProcessPoolExecutor, because processes don't have a GIL limitation on network calls
Neither — use a single thread since downloads must happen one at a time
ProcessPoolExecutor, because more workers = more speed always
ThreadPoolExecutor, because this is I/O-bound — the GIL releases during network waits, letting waits overlap
